claims.text: THE CREDENTIAL CASE AGAINST LAZAR WAS MADE BY A UFO PROPONENT, NOT A DEBUNKER, AND THAT IS THE PART THE LITERATURE LOSES. Friedman, a nuclear physicist who spent his career arguing that UFOs are real craft, wrote 'The Bob Lazar Fraud' in December 1997, updated January 2011: 'No diplomas, no resumes, no transcripts, no memberships in professional organizations, no papers, no pages from MIT or Caltech yearbooks.' On the schools: 'Pierce said he had taken electronics courses in the late 1970s. The other three schools never heard of him.' On the professor Lazar named as a Caltech instructor: 'I located Dr. Duxler. He's a Pierce Junior College physics prof, and never taught at Caltech.' Duxler checked his own records and told Friedman that Lazar had taken at least one of his Pierce classes in the late 1970s.

claims.text: On the two documents most often cited in Lazar's favour, Friedman, who had seen both, records what they actually show. On the W-2: 'His W-2 form from the Department of Naval Intelligence totals under $1000.00, at most a week's pay for a scientist.' On the Los Alamos directory: 'The page from the Los Alamos National Lab phone book with Lazar's name on it clearly states that it includes employees of the DOE and outside contractor, Kirk Meyer.' On element 115: 'It has a very short half life so there is no way to accumulate pounds of it.'

claims.source: Headquarters USAF, 'The Roswell Report: Fact versus Fiction in the New Mexico Desert' (1995) https://archive.org/details/DTIC_ADA326148
claims.text: The US Air Force's own 1995 Roswell report states: 'In 1978, a UFO researcher, Stanton Friedman, met with Marcel and began investigating the claims that the material Marcel handled was from a crashed UFO.' The board's account of Friedman as the first civilian investigator to reach Marcel is therefore attested by the Air Force, not only by Friedman.

claims.source: Headquarters USAF, 'The Roswell Report: Fact versus Fiction in the New Mexico Desert' (1995), review of the popular literature https://archive.org/details/DTIC_ADA326148
claims.text: The same report lists 'Crash at Corona (1992) by Stanton T. Friedman and Don Berliner' among the major works its records search reviewed, placing Friedman's authorship in the Air Force's own bibliography of the case.

Friedman's 'Top Secret/MAJIC' was published by Marlowe & Co. in 1996, ISBN 1569248303, and is available as a full scan. The board's claim about his Hillenkoetter-memo analysis cited this book by title with no locator.

CBC News reports that Friedman died suddenly at Toronto Pearson Airport on the Monday night of 13 May 2019, aged 84, while returning from a speaking engagement in Columbus, Ohio, and describes him as 'a nuclear physicist by training' who 'had devoted his life to researching and investigating UFOs since the late 1960s'. The City of Fredericton declared 27 August 2007 Stanton Friedman Day.

meta.speaker: Joanna Aiton-Kerr (Provincial Archives of New Brunswick), per CBC News

claims.text: Friedman began donating his research collection to the Provincial Archives of New Brunswick in the months before his death. Archivist Joanna Aiton-Kerr told CBC the archives had received about 300 boxes -- roughly 60 metres laid end to end -- and expected several more cargo vans. This is where the primary material behind his Roswell and MJ-12 work now sits, and it is not online.

claimsMade.text: THE QUALIFICATION, WHICH TRAVELS WITH THE ARTICLE AND IS ROUTINELY DROPPED. The description is what Lazar told the reporter, not an employment record. Stanton Friedman, who obtained the Los Alamos telephone directory page carrying Lazar's name, records that the page 'clearly states that it includes employees of the DOE and outside contractor, Kirk Meyer'. A Los Alamos colleague interviewed on tape by Mark Farmer on 25 May 1996 said Lazar 'was a contractor' under 'Kirk Mayer' and that he 'claimed to be' a physicist. Tom Mahood's 2018 conclusion is that Lazar worked as an electronic technician for Kirk-Mayer and that the Monitor article misrepresented his position on the basis of what he told the reporter.

conflicts: Friedman defended the authenticity of the core MJ-12 documents; Kevin Randle ('Conclusions on Operation Majestic Twelve', 1994; 'Case MJ-12', 2002), Philip Klass and the FBI's 'BOGUS' annotation on the Aquarius/Cutler-Twining material took the opposite view. This dispute is unresolved and is recorded on this board as unresolved.

label: Stanton T. Friedman
narrative: Stanton Terry Friedman (29 July 1934 - 13 May 2019) was a nuclear physicist who spent fourteen years on classified nuclear propulsion programmes at General Electric, Aerojet General Nucleonics, General Motors, Westinghouse, TRW and McDonnell Douglas before leaving full-time physics in 1970 to investigate UFOs professionally. That industrial background matters to this board: Friedman had held clearances on compartmented nuclear aircraft and fission and fusion rocket work, and he argued from direct experience that a programme could be run for decades without leaking, because he had worked inside ones that did not. In February 1978 in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, he was put in touch with Major Jesse A. Marcel Sr., the 509th Bomb Group intelligence officer who had handled the Roswell debris - the single act that restarted the Roswell case after thirty years of silence and made him, as he put it, the first civilian to document the site. He fed Marcel to William Moore and Charles Berlitz, whose 1980 'The Roswell Incident' made the case public. From 1984 he was the principal defender of the Majestic 12 documents received by Moore and Jaime Shandera, publishing 'Top Secret/Majic' in 1996 and maintaining that no substantive grounds existed for dismissing the authenticity of the core documents - a position that split him permanently from Randle, Klass and much of the field. He was also the first to demonstrate that some MJ-12 papers were provably faked, showing that a purported 17 February 1948 Hillenkoetter-to-Truman memo was an emulation of a Marshall-to-Roosevelt letter reproduced in 'The American MAGIC'. He testified in writing to a House committee in 1968, appeared twice at the United Nations, and donated his research files to the Provincial Archives of New Brunswick shortly before his death.

timeline.label: Friedman meets Marcel
timeline.text: Stanton Friedman is put in touch with retired Lt. Col. Jesse Marcel Sr. in Baton Rouge. Marcel states the weather balloon account was a cover and that the material was not of this earth. Roswell restarts after thirty-one years.

timeline.label: Friedman dies
